comments.author: @michaelcushman
comments.text:
A better example of a parallel job to programmers is Word Processing. 

First there were typists, millions of them. 

Second, word processing machines and the specialists, highly trained, word processors, who could fix mistakes with a keystroke, essentially typeset an document, digitally. Typists still existed, but everyone was saying, learn WP.

Third, the PC goes global, WP software is cheap, then bundled. Anyone can digitally create documents, fix their own mistakes, typeset... although slower and less professionally than WPs. 

The big change was taking out wait time. Instead of submitting WP work into a queue and waiting, then proofreading, resubmitting correction ... people could do it themselves, when needed. 
The job, WP disappeared fast, within 5 years.

AI is do it yourself coding. Not as good as a pro, but no waiting. No requests to IT, no lobbying to give it priority, no out of pocket costs to 3rd parties. 

The spreadsheet example isnt as relevant, because spreadsheets didnt do accounting, it did tables.  Spreadsheets are equivalent to IDEs.

AI DOES does programming. It enables DIY for the masses. Not as good as professionals, but no waiting, no begging, no out of pocket costs.

comments.author: @Grumpy_Rabbit
comments.text:
LLMs don't do new research. They're not embodied, so they can't. They compute theorems that are derivable from the axioms, and generate consensus summaries of whatever is claimed/recommended in their training data. And they're subject to the "map is not the territory" problem, and to Gödel's Incompleteness Theorems. 

LLMs work by generating the most probable responses found in their training data. Human-level intelligence goes beyond that: It functions as a hierarchy of surprisal-based signal propagation, in a self-referential feedback loop. That's the opposite of how LLMs work. And that's why humans can discover solutions such as the null hypothesis, the scientific method, Bayesian inference and pan-critical rationalism: We think "outside the box" in ways that can't be duplicated simply by computing theorems derivable from the rules of the system (logic, math, other formal systems or rules.)

Humans challenge authority. LLM's don't: They regurgitate it as gospel--and by design, they define "authority" as "what's the most probable claim/assertion" encountered in their training data.

LLMs are the digital equivalent of a stereotypical bureaucrat, who always follows the rules, regardless of how ridiculous they may be.

comments.author: @scotttaylor9133
comments.text:
I think that most fields would suffer from the same issues that would plague adoption in software.  

The real issue is the lack of any actual understanding conceptually of anything, so for anything beyond very simple coding tasks done at a mediocre level, it's just not great.  So it may help, MAYBE, except it's a guessing machine, and have no idea if its guesses are right or wrong (unless you actually know, and then you wouldn't need it).  For software in particular, it's stochastic in nature and not idempotent, meaning you won't get the same code out twice.  The only way I see to overcome this would be COMPLETE testing suites, automated, to test every function.  And those HAVE to be right (you'd be betting the farm on them).  You also have to know every potential use case and corner case to avoid regressions.  Once you have that (I've never seen a company with that btw), then you could use the training data, multiple passes and reinforcement to have it generate working systems (as opposed to just code snips or boilerplate).  The problem there is that you will very likely end up with human readable code.  Conventions will be thrown aside, randomization will take hold as it iterates to try and pass the tests and optimize for nfrs.  Meaning that, again, you can't debug it, and you don't have a stable product.

I work in software, but I think that every field has flavors of these problems.  I think it's great for auto complete, it's great even for a short chat partner (which says a lot about us).  To date we haven't seen an AI capable of writing coherent scripts for even small episodes of shows.  And it's all back to the same problem.  Fundamentally, these are either self adjusting iteration based randomized systems that require success conditions, or just essentially guessing the next word.  Neither of those two will get you out stable work that can be relied upon.  Software is probably the easiest place to get this to work since you can run multiple iterations without any problems.  Medical?  Legal?  The patient can only die once, and the case is only heard once.  I think the same extends to most fields out there.

I think this is wildly over hyped, and it's really something more like a next generation search engine, or a really good pattern recognition system.  Beyond that, I don't think we're remotely close to having anything with conceptual understanding.  We have a really sophisticated, really good magic eight ball.

In planning your career path, 3 things have traditionally had the biggest impact on your financial success:
 
1) What work you do.
2) How good you are at doing it.
3) How many other people are doing it.
 
In an AI world, my bet is software development will trend towards more automation and likely more natural language programming: the actual hard coding will become less important than accurately describing what exactly it is you want to achieve, with AI tools prompting you for clarification, providing options, suggestions etc. It may years to get there, but I suspect that we will always need software developers...just WAY fewer than are currently in the pipeline and that their skillset will need to be somewhat different.
